c018d938.1.text:
Primero las respuestas cortas: yo mantendría "AI" en ese título, cambiaría a "Resume" solo si apuntás principalmente a trabajos de EE. UU., y no, el sitio no detecta el idioma.

**1. "How I work with AI" → "My usual workflow"**

Yo no haría este cambio. El título nuevo saca "AI", y esa palabra es lo que distingue a la sección. También es lo que busca un reclutador que escanea la página. "Usual" la hace sonar vaga e informal. La sección trata de la configuración que armaste alrededor del agente, no de tu rutina en general.

Si querés algo más corto o menos formal, estas opciones mantienen el sentido:
- **"How I build with AI"** (mi elección: es activa y encaja con "builds agents and robots")
- "My AI workflow"
- "Working with AI agents"

El título aparece en cinco lugares: la navegación principal, la lista de partes, la etiqueta del riel, el encabezado de la sección en el inicio y el encabezado propio de la página. Es un cambio rápido elijas la que elijas.

**2. "CV" → "Resume"**

Depende de a quién quieras llegar:
- **EE. UU. y Canadá:** "Resume" es la palabra habitual. Ahí, "CV" suele significar un documento académico largo.
- **Reino Unido, Europa y Latinoamérica:** "CV" es lo normal.

Apuntás a trabajos remotos. Si la mayoría son empresas de EE. UU., usá **"Resume"**. Si el objetivo es más amplio, mantené "CV": es más corto y todos lo entienden. Elijas lo que elijas, lo usaría en todos lados: navegación, título de la página, el link "CV (PDF)" y la URL (`/resume/`, con `/cv/` redirigiendo ahí). ¿A qué mercado apuntás principalmente?

**3. Detección de idioma**

No. El sitio es solo en inglés (`lang="en"`), que es la política de idioma de `BRIEF.md` §3. Lo único en español va a ser la conversación del build en P4, mostrada en el original con una traducción opcional al inglés.

La detección automática implicaría escribir y mantener una versión en español de cada página, lo cual es un gran cambio de alcance. Si alguna vez querés español, agregaría un selector manual EN/ES con páginas `/es/` en lugar de redirigir automáticamente. Las redirecciones automáticas molestan a quienes leen en inglés con un navegador en español, y confunden a los motores de búsqueda.

Decime qué título y qué redacción de CV/Resume querés, y aplico las dos en la rama `p3-layout`.

## 1. What the research says (what the sources agree on)

I read about 15 sources from 2026 (recruiter guides, hiring-manager checklists, HN, Reddit) and almost all of them agree on this:

- **The quick review lasts between 10 and 60 seconds.** On the first screen it has to be clear what you do, for what role and how to contact you. Then the recruiter opens a project and looks for a demo, the code and a README.
- **Show 3 to 5 projects as case studies, not as a gallery.** Each with the problem, the decision you made, **what you did** in a team project, the constraints you had and what you would change. The most repeated mistake is showing the result without explaining the reasoning.
- **A pretty UI no longer differentiates.** With AI anyone has it. Animations that delay the information count against you.
- **The "About" goes in two paragraphs.** The personal origin is told once and short; it's not the protagonist.

## 2. Trends and where to stand out

- **Already saturated:** the terminal/ASCII/monospaced aesthetic and the "chat with my resume". The latter has a lukewarm reception: in a Show HN the criticism was that "recruiters spend seconds anyway; the chat doesn't change that".
- **Your best differentiator is the section with the chat with the agent, and it's aligned with the industry.** According to HN and the press, the YC S26 form asks for *"Attach a coding agent session you're particularly proud of"*. Tools to export and replay sessions already exist (`claude-replay`, `ai-sessions`, ThreadCast, SpecStory). It's not an invented idea: it's something the industry is starting to ask for.
- **Your second differentiator is your profile.** Few portfolios cover robotics and kinematics, PLC, Elixir/OTP, Rust/Tauri, voice AI and tools for agents. I suggest something like "I work in software and hardware", told with evidence and without adjectives.

## 3. My recommendations on your ideas

**Chat of how you made the page.** Yes, as a central piece.
- The format: a player that advances on its own, pauses on click and from there you read the full transcript, with chapters and the tool calls collapsed.
- Two things to keep in mind:
  1. A real session has a huge amount of noise. It needs to be curated without editing your messages: choose chapters and collapse, never rewrite.
  2. Sensitive data (paths, email, keys) has to be hidden.
- This session can be "chapter 0: direction". Pi stores sessions in JSONL, so the prompt will ask for them to be kept.

**Language.** I recommend **the page in English and the transcript in the original Spanish, with an optional translation alongside.**

**AI-generated decoration.** One LLM call per visit has concrete risks:
- Free tiers (Groq, Workers AI, Gemini) get exhausted by bots.
- It adds latency.
- Inserting live-generated SVG opens the door to XSS.

The realistic option is a **bank of pieces generated once a day (cron) and cached**, with a visible label: "generated today by <model>, prompt: …". The AI is noticeable and transparent. - **The photo** is in `media/photos/2004_first-computer_01.jpg`, copied unchanged.
- **The CV** is in `inputs/cv/resume.tex`. That folder isn't uploaded to the repository because it has your phone number. I renamed the old `inputs/linkedin/` to `inputs/cv/` and updated the `.gitignore`, the brief and the pending list.

## The photo

It's a good photo for this: you look focused, with both hands on the keyboard, and it tells the story without needing to explain it.

- **Smaller: yes.** Between 280 and 360 px wide, and if needed cropped toward you and the keyboard.
- **Improving it with AI: I don't recommend it.** Models that upscale resolution invent detail, especially on faces, and a regenerated child's face usually looks odd. It also goes against the central idea of the page: showing how you really made it, without makeup. A light cleanup that doesn't invent anything is fine: a bit of noise reduction, white balance and exposure.
- **Blurred edges: no either.** That effect looks dated. A printed-photo-style frame or a subtle color treatment that matches the palette looks better; the specific style is chosen in the design phase (P2).

I left all this noted in `photos.yaml`, along with an alt text in English. **You still need to write the caption**: one line in your own words, in Spanish or in English.

I couldn't check whether the photo still has location metadata, because I don't have the tool to read it installed. It's a WhatsApp copy, and WhatsApp usually strips it; even so, the build removes it.

## The CV: three things that change the brief

1. **The phone number isn't published.** The PDF downloaded from the page is generated from a public version of your CV, without the phone number. The LaTeX format you already prepared for automated CV filters (ATS) is respected.
2. **It's now a good idea to add GitHub to the CV.** The comment in your `.tex` says you removed it because your code was on a private GitLab. With this page's repo being public, that changes; the public PDF includes it.
3. **Your CV data takes precedence over what the agents summarized.** The agent had said EmprendER was a team of 3. Your CV says you're the biggest contributor (353 of 766 commits), the only developer since March, and that you closed an access-control flaw. That makes it a strong candidate to feature later.

About MTDS: in your CV you said that you demonstrated that the remote center of motion (RCM) was unreachable with the hardware built and that you reported that negative result instead of simulating it. It's exactly the reasoning part that, according to recruiters, is most missing in portfolios, so the brief will use it as the axis of that case study.

All you're missing is the photo caption, and you can write it during the build session. With that you can start with the message I gave you.
